title: The Science of Emotions
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
A feeling tells us that something matters to the person experiencing it. It does not, by itself, establish which explanation of an event is true.

How do we listen to an emotion without letting it make every decision?
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: What emotion means
nodes.body:
A response that organises attention and prepares us to react when something feels important.

For example: Anger rises after a colleague makes a decision about someone's work without including them.

One important limit: The strength of a feeling is not a measure of the other person's intention.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: Anger rises after a colleague makes a decision about someone's work without including them. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports emotion. A response that organises attention and prepares us to react when something feels important. The strength of a feeling is not a measure of the other person's intention.
nodes.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Appraisal.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Action urge.
options.feedback: Action urge is a genuine psychological idea, but the observation by itself does not establish it. An urge is information about readiness to act, not an instruction that must be followed.

options.label: This most directly illustrates Emotion regulation.
options.feedback: Emotion regulation is a genuine psychological idea, but the observation by itself does not establish it. Regulation is not identical to suppressing a feeling or pretending it is unimportant.

options.label: The case requires at least two of these concepts to explain the observed event.

nodes.title: What action urge means
nodes.body:
The thing a feeling makes us want to do immediately.

For example: After feeling excluded, somebody wants to send an accusatory message.

One important limit: An urge is information about readiness to act, not an instruction that must be followed.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: What emotion regulation means
nodes.body:
Changing how we respond to a feeling, or the conditions influencing it, to serve a longer-term goal.

For example: Someone waits until they have enough information before writing to the meeting organiser.

One important limit: Regulation is not identical to suppressing a feeling or pretending it is unimportant.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Nora discovers she was left off a meeting invitation where a project decision was made. She tells Felix afterwards.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.
nodes.scenario: Nora discovers she was left off a meeting invitation where a project decision was made. She tells Felix afterwards.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm furious. They made the decision without me.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That sounds frustrating. Do you know why you weren't invited?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No. I want to send a message saying they deliberately excluded me.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What tells you it was deliberate?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
checks.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

items.label: “I'm furious. They made the decision without me.”
Anger may register an appraisal of unfairness and energise a response. It communicates how Nora experiences the situation, while the cause of the exclusion remains uncertain.
“That sounds frustrating. Do you know why you weren't invited?”
There may be a recurring exclusionary practice, in which case her concern could accurately reflect a wider workplace problem.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Anger may register an appraisal of unfairness and energise a response. It communicates how Nora experiences the situation, while the cause of the exclusion remains uncertain.

Another possibility: There may be a recurring exclusionary practice, in which case her concern could accurately reflect a wider workplace problem.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Examine the invitation process and whether relevant colleagues are routinely omitted. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Examine the invitation process and whether relevant colleagues are routinely omitted.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: A calendar audit shows the invite list was copied from an old meeting that predates Nora's involvement.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: An administrative explanation now has direct support. Her concern about having influence remains legitimate even if exclusion was accidental.
nodes.counterexample: Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (2015), emotion regulation framework.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: What does the anger point to?
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of a feeling is information not a verdict.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Emotions are partly shaped by how events affect a person's goals. Anger can draw attention to an obstructed expectation, such as being consulted in a shared decision. The feeling provides information about what matters to Amir; it does not itself establish Jess's intention.

Past experiences and immediate context can alter emotional appraisals. Anger alone is not reliable evidence about another person's motives.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (1998), emotion regulation.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Lazarus (1991), Emotion and Adaptation; Gross (1998), emotion regulation.
nodes.scenario: Jess booked a trip date without checking with Amir, who expected to decide together.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm angry that you booked it without asking.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I thought you'd said either weekend was okay.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I meant either weekend could work, not that we'd chosen.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I didn't mean to leave you out.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I believe you. I still feel as though I wasn't part of the decision.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Then let's work out how we choose these things next time.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A person feels intense jealousy when their partner meets a friend. The feeling reveals what matters to them but cannot establish whether a betrayal occurred.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

options.label: Explain the impact of missing the meeting and propose an explicit procedure for involving project contributors.
options.feedback: It addresses recurrence; it may be premature to prescribe a procedure without knowing why the omission occurred.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Anger may register an appraisal of unfairness and energise a response. It communicates how Nora experiences the situation, while the cause of the exclusion remains uncertain.

Emotions can be informative without verifying the thoughts attached to them. Suppressing the feeling is not the same as evaluating the interpretation.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.

glossary.definition: A response that organises attention and prepares us to react when something feels important.
glossary.example: Anger rises after a colleague makes a decision about someone's work without including them.
glossary.limit: The strength of a feeling is not a measure of the other person's intention.

glossary.definition: The meaning we give to an event, such as interpreting it as unfair or threatening.
glossary.example: Being left off a meeting invitation is read as a deliberate slight.
glossary.limit: An appraisal may fit the facts, or it may change when new information arrives.

glossary.definition: The thing a feeling makes us want to do immediately.
glossary.example: After feeling excluded, somebody wants to send an accusatory message.
glossary.limit: An urge is information about readiness to act, not an instruction that must be followed.

glossary.definition: Changing how we respond to a feeling, or the conditions influencing it, to serve a longer-term goal.
glossary.example: Someone waits until they have enough information before writing to the meeting organiser.
glossary.limit: Regulation is not identical to suppressing a feeling or pretending it is unimportant.
